title: Substitution and ellipsis
tagline: Say it once — then let so, one, do so and a bare 'to' carry the rest.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (so, not, one, do, to)
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (so, not, one, the same)
Speaking Parts 1-4 — natural short answers instead of repeating a whole clause
Writing Part 2 — fluent narrative without clumsy repetition
why: Fluent English avoids saying the same words twice. Substitution words like so, one and the same replace a whole idea, and ellipsis simply leaves out what the listener or reader can already recover — 'I'd like to (go)', 'She can (swim), and so can I'. C1 Advanced tests this constantly, in the open cloze and in key word transformations, and a text that keeps repeating full clauses instead of using so/not, do so or a well-placed gap reads as noticeably less fluent than one that doesn't.

diagrams.title: Avoiding repetition: substitution and ellipsis

before.text: I think it will rain tomorrow, and my sister thinks it will rain tomorrow too.
hl: thinks it will rain tomorrow too

after.text: I think it will rain tomorrow, and my sister thinks so too.

steps: Find the repeated clause (it will rain tomorrow).
Replace it with 'so' after verbs like think/hope/suppose/expect, or drop it completely after an auxiliary.
Keep the rest of the sentence unchanged.

branches.label: do so / did so
items: She left early, and he did so too

branches.label: one / ones
items: I need a pen — do you have one?

branches.label: ellipsis after auxiliaries / to
items: She can (swim), and so can I

branches.label: if so / if not
items: shorthand for a whole preceding condition

rows.label: Verb phrase
cells: She wanted to leave, and I wanted to leave too.
She wanted to leave, and I wanted to too.

rows.label: Whole clause
cells: I think it will work, and he thinks it will work.
I think it will work, and he thinks so.

rows.label: Noun
cells: I lost my pen, so I bought a new pen.
I lost my pen, so I bought a new one.

rows.label: Effect
cells: correct, but repetitive and unnatural at C1
fluent — a clear sign of native-like economy

use.point: so and not after verbs of thinking and hoping

examples.text: 'Is Mateo coming to the trip?' 'I think so.'
examples.note: think + so replaces 'that Mateo is coming'
afraid + so, a polite way of confirming bad news

examples.text: 'Will the results be published today?' 'I hope not.'

use.point: do so / did so, and one/ones

examples.text: Nadia submitted her project early, and Liam did so as well.
examples.note: did so replaces 'submitted his project early', formal register

examples.text: The old textbooks were replaced with new ones this term.
examples.note: ones replaces the plural countable noun 'textbooks'

examples.text: If you need a calculator, there's a spare one in the drawer.
Sofia hasn't finished her essay yet, but Nadia has.
examples.note: ellipsis of 'finished her essay' after the auxiliary

examples.text: 'Are you coming to the concert?' 'I'd like to, but I can't.'
examples.note: 'to' stands for the whole infinitive 'to come to the concert'

examples.text: He can speak French fluently, and so can his sister.

use.point: Omitting repeated subjects, verbs and relative pronouns

examples.text: Mateo cleared the table and washed the dishes.
examples.note: the repeated subject 'Mateo' is dropped before the second verb

examples.text: The essay she submitted last week won the prize.
examples.note: 'that/which' can be omitted when it's the object of the relative clause

examples.text: 'If so, we'll leave at six; if not, we'll wait for the bus.'
examples.note: if so / if not stand for a whole condition already stated

watch_out.why: 'It' cannot replace a whole clause after think/hope/suppose — use 'so' (or 'not' for the negative).

watch_out.wrong: She left early, and he did it so too.
watch_out.right: She left early, and he did so too.
watch_out.why: 'Do so' is a fixed formal phrase — don't add 'it' inside it.

watch_out.wrong: I lost my pen, so I bought a new.
watch_out.right: I lost my pen, so I bought a new one.
watch_out.why: After an adjective, a singular countable noun needs 'one' to stand in for it — you can't just drop it.

watch_out.wrong: She can't come, but I can to.
watch_out.why: After a modal or auxiliary, the rest of the verb phrase is simply dropped — don't add 'to'.

watch_out.wrong: I didn't want to go, but I felt I ought.
watch_out.right: I didn't want to go, but I felt I ought to.
watch_out.why: After 'ought', the bare ellipted infinitive still needs 'to'; only the main verb is omitted.

watch_out.wrong: Are you free tomorrow? If, let's meet.
watch_out.right: Are you free tomorrow? If so, let's meet.
watch_out.why: 'If' alone can't stand for the whole condition — it must be 'if so' or 'if not'.

dialogue.title: Sorting out the weekend
dialogue.context: Mateo, Sofia, Liam and Nadia are messaging about a trip to the coast, using natural short answers instead of repeating whole sentences.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Is the bus leaving at seven or eight?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I think so — seven, I mean. Liam confirmed it yesterday.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: I did, yes. Also, does anyone still need a wetsuit? There's a spare one at my house.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I could use one, actually — mine is too small now.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Great. Sofia, are you bringing snacks?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I'd like to, but I haven't had time to shop yet.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: No worries, I'll do so instead — I'm passing the supermarket anyway.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Is the weather supposed to be good on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I hope so. The forecast said sunny, but I'm not sure it's reliable.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: If so, we should leave early to get the best spot on the beach.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Agreed. And if not, we'll just bring the tent instead.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Either way, I can't wait — see you all at six thirty!

summary: So and not replace a whole clause after think, hope, suppose, expect and be afraid: I think so, I'm afraid not.
Do so / did so replaces a whole verb phrase in formal writing; one/ones replaces a countable noun already mentioned.
After an auxiliary or modal, the rest of the verb phrase can simply be dropped: She can't come, but I can.
After verbs like want to, need to, ought to, the bare to stands for the whole infinitive that follows.
If so / if not stand for a whole condition already stated — a fast, natural way to link two sentences.
